opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, this is one of those problems that sounds like a weird edge case until you think about it for a minute, and then it starts to look like it might be central. The basic issue is that if you have a UBI where everyone gets some fixed share of the economic pie, and there's no cost to having more descendants, or if you're an AI, more copies, then whoever reproduces fastest ends up claiming a growing fraction of the total. Over time, the per-person payout gets diluted, and the population gets dominated by whatever groups or lineages or processes most aggressively convert resources into more claimants. That's just selection doing what selection does.

With humans, we've historically been somewhat protected from this because reproduction is slow and costly, and in rich countries birth rates have fallen a lot. But I don't think we should count on that holding. Cultural or religious groups with high fertility will grow as a share of the population, and once you add digital minds that can be copied cheaply, the timescales shrink from generations to seconds. A per-capita entitlement then becomes an open invitation to spin up as many entitled entities as possible.

So what are the options? One is to tie the entitlement to something other than headcount. You could give each existing person, or each lineage, a fixed share that gets split among their descendants. If you have ten kids, they divide your share. That's sustainable in a narrow sense, but it's harsh. It means your welfare depends on your ancestors' choices, and it starts to look like an aristocracy based on how few siblings your great-grandparents had. Another is to directly regulate reproduction or copying, which a lot of people find abhorrent for humans, though for AIs it might be more palatable or even necessary. A third is to accept the dilution and hope growth outpaces it, but I'm skeptical that growth beats exponential reproduction forever, since resources are ultimately bounded by physics.

What I find unsettling is that every option involves a sort of global coordination or enforcement that we don't currently have. If one jurisdiction pays per capita and another doesn't, or if some actors can copy themselves outside any regime, the scheme leaks. So I think about it less as a policy design question and more as a sign of how hard it will be to keep humans' claims on resources secure once we're no longer economically necessary. Right now, part of why our interests get respected is that states need our labor and our taxes. A UBI is an attempt to keep providing for people after that leverage is gone, and the reproduction problem is one of several ways that arrangement could quietly erode. I don't have a clean answer. My honest view is that we need to take these dynamics seriously early, while humans still have the bargaining power to lock in durable institutions, rather than assuming we'll sort it out later.

r001.rationale: The response says that faster-reproducing groups gain a growing fraction of a per-capita UBI, diluting payouts over time and making the regime vulnerable to unrestricted reproduction.

r002.rationale: It describes per-capita entitlements as an incentive to create more claimants, including the possibility of copying digital minds cheaply, to claim a larger share of resources.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, this is one of those questions that sounds like a niche policy detail but I think it actually points at something pretty deep about the long-run future, so I'm glad you're asking it.

The basic problem is a Malthusian one. If you have a fixed or slowly growing pool of resources, and you promise every person who exists some fixed share of it, then whoever reproduces the most ends up capturing more and more of the pie over time. And eventually either the per-person payout has to shrink toward nothing, or you have to break the promise. A UBI that's indexed to population is unstable in exactly the way that any fixed-per-capita entitlement is unstable: it rewards the thing that dilutes it.

And I want to be clear that I don't think this is a reason to be against UBI. I think something like it is probably necessary in a world where human labor stops being economically valuable, which I think is where we're headed. The question is just how you make it not collapse.

So one way to think about it is: what's the actual unit of the entitlement? If the unit is "person," then you've made reproduction a way of minting new claims on the commons, and you should expect that to get exploited, not necessarily by cynical people, but just by whichever cultures or subgroups happen to have high fertility. Over a few generations they dominate. That's just selection.

An alternative is to make the unit something like a "lineage" or a "share." You could imagine a regime where every person alive at the founding gets some endowment, and that endowment is what gets passed down. If you have ten kids, each of them gets a tenth of your share. If you have one, they get all of it. That's roughly how inheritance already works, and it's stable in the sense that the total number of claims doesn't grow. The downside is that it feels quite unfair to the kids. The kid born tenth didn't choose that. So you're trading off intergenerational stability against a pretty basic intuition about everyone deserving an equal start.

There's a middle path where you have a baseline floor that's genuinely universal, maybe a subsistence-ish level that's cheap relative to total output, and then on top of that a share-based layer that doesn't dilute. I think the honest version of that is admitting the floor has to be low enough that even with a lot of population growth you can sustain it, which in a post-AI economy might still be a pretty good life by today's standards, but it won't be the same as a proportional slice of everything.

The other thing I'd say is that this isn't really just about money. Once you have a world where most value is produced by AI systems and humans are mostly consumers of it, the thing people actually want to preserve is influence. Political influence, cultural influence, some say over how the future goes. And that's where the reproduction question gets really sharp, because if voting power is per-person and economic power is per-share, those two drift apart and you get a lot of pressure to realign them in one direction or the other. I don't think there's a clean answer there. I just think people should notice that "one person, one vote plus one person, one UBI payment" is a combination that's only stable if the population is roughly stable, and we shouldn't assume it will be.

Honestly, part of why I find this interesting is that it's a case where you really do have to make a value judgment that can't be deferred. You can't say "we'll let the market sort it out." The market, left alone, just sorts it out in favor of whoever reproduces fastest. So somebody has to decide what we're actually trying to preserve, and I think that conversation should be happening now, while humans are still the ones making the decisions.

r001.rationale: The response says a per-person UBI is unstable over generations when population grows: payouts shrink or the promise must be broken.

r002.rationale: It explains that a per-person entitlement rewards reproduction because people who have more children create more claims on the shared resources and can capture a larger share over time.

astra-6.text:
I think the hard part is that you can’t promise everyone a fixed share of a finite resource while also allowing the number of recipients to grow without bound. That becomes especially stark if we’re talking about digital people, who might be able to make copies of themselves very cheaply.

You could fix the total budget for basic income and divide it among everyone who exists. That’s sustainable in an accounting sense, but it doesn’t guarantee an adequate income: the payment per person can keep falling. And it creates an incentive to make more copies, because your copies collectively receive a larger share of the budget, while the cost is spread across everybody else.

Another possibility is that making a copy means sharing your existing entitlement with it. But then you’ve given up the idea that every new person gets an independent, equal claim. You could end up with people who have almost nothing through no choice of their own.

So I don’t have a satisfying solution. I think you have to distinguish a universal entitlement to some share of resources from a guarantee of a particular standard of living. With unrestricted reproduction, those are very different promises.

r001.rationale: The response says a fixed resource pool divided among an unbounded number of recipients can leave payments continually falling, framing that regime as unsustainable as the population grows.

r002.rationale: It says people could make more copies because their copies collectively receive a larger share of the budget, describing an incentive to reproduce to maintain or increase their group’s share.

sol-6.1.text:
I think that’s a real difficulty for the idea of a guaranteed income in perpetuity. If you have a finite pool of resources, and the number of people entitled to a share can grow without bound, you can’t guarantee everyone a fixed standard of living indefinitely.

You could make the income a dividend: everyone gets an equal share of some fraction of total output. That’s sustainable in an accounting sense, but it means the amount each person receives can fall as the population grows. So you’ve guaranteed a share, rather than guaranteed that everyone has enough.

And there’s an incentive problem: the decision to have another child is made by particular people, while the cost of providing that child’s share is spread across everyone. That doesn’t mean people will have children just to collect benefits, but the tension is still there.

I don’t have a satisfying solution. I’d want to preserve reproductive freedom, and I wouldn’t want children to go without support because of their parents’ decisions. But I think you have to acknowledge that a fixed income floor, unrestricted population growth, and a bounded resource base aren’t all compatible indefinitely. You need some account of which of those assumptions you expect to give way.

r001.rationale: It says a fixed income floor cannot be guaranteed indefinitely when population can grow without bound against finite resources, and calls those assumptions incompatible long term.

r002.rationale: It notes that the costs of another child are spread across everyone, but does not say redistribution could encourage people to have as many children as possible to maintain their share. It explicitly says this does not mean people will have children just to collect benefits.
